displayQuote: Youth is wasted on the young

meta.title: Who really said "Youth is wasted on the young"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: George Bernard Shaw never wrote it. The line grew out of unsourced 1931 newspaper columns that credited Shaw with a looser phrase — the crisp version is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Youth is wasted on the young'?
meta.ogDescription: Not documented in Shaw's works. It crystallized from 1931 newspaper wit credited to Shaw in a different wording — the modern phrase appeared unattributed.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — an unsourced 1931 newspaper saying
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment was pinned on Shaw in North American newspapers in 1931, but always in looser wording (“what a pity it has to be wasted on children”) — and researchers have never found the line in anything he actually wrote. A December 1931 Massachusetts paper carried an unattributed but still looser variant (“so much youth is wasted on young people”), and the exact phrasing “youth is wasted on the young” is not documented until 1945 — so the crisp modern wording is a later refinement, not a documented Shaw quotation.

source.heading: Where the saying actually comes from

docMeta.dd: A looser form — “so much youth is wasted on young people” — credited to the Springfield Union
Not documented until 1945 (Ann Pinchot: “a pity youth is wasted on the young”)

source.excerpt: “Youth,” he replied, “is the most beautiful thing in this world—and what a pity that it has to be wasted on children!”
trail: The earliest strong matches appear in 1931 newspaper columns, credited to Shaw but worded as “what a pity it has to be wasted on children.”

A looser, unattributed variant — “so much youth is wasted on young people” — shows up in a December 1931 Massachusetts paper, credited only to the Springfield Union; the exact phrasing “youth is wasted on the young” is not documented until 1945 (Ann Pinchot).
Wiktionary notes the phrase “is often attributed to…George Bernard Shaw…but does not appear to be from any of his published works,” and is also pinned on Twain and Wilde.
Wikiquote’s Shaw page does not carry this line in any of its sourced, attributed, disputed, or misattributed sections.
source.excerptNote: The February 1931 version credited to Shaw in Ted Cook’s column — the sentiment, but not the familiar wording. The polished “youth is wasted on the young” came later.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous, refined form of a saying that circulated in the 1931 press; no identifiable author or specific pre-existing work can be tied to it, so no copyright status is asserted. Shaw’s own writings do not contain the line.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: About George Bernard Shaw
author.bio: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish dramatist and critic whose plays — Pygmalion, Man and Superman, Saint Joan — paired wit with social argument, and who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925. His genuine epigrams are so quotable that he has become one of the internet’s great magnets for invented one-liners. This is one of them: the paradox about youth suits his voice, but it was newspaper wits, not Shaw’s pen, that put it into circulation.

cite.sourceCitation: Garson O’Toole (Gregory F. Sullivan), “Youth Is Wasted on the Young,” Quote Investigator, September 7, 2015. misattribution.heading: How Shaw got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is a textbook “magnet-name” quote: a clever paradox that drifted onto a famous wit’s name and hardened into a household saying, even though the wording is nobody’s documented sentence.

items.why: 1931 humor columns did credit Shaw — but with looser phrasing like “the most beautiful thing…wasted on children.” Researchers have never found the adage in Shaw’s writings, and the exact modern form appeared unattributed.
By 1963 the saying was also being handed to Wilde without support — a common fate when a quip needs a quotable Irishman, as Wiktionary notes.
Wiktionary records that the line is “sometimes also said to be by” Mark Twain — another famous wit who attracts orphan quotations, with no evidence he said it.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: an unsourced 1931 newspaper saying, credited to Shaw in a different wording and refined by later re-quoting — not a line found in Shaw, Wilde, or Twain, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the wording keeps changing
lead: Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the idea mutating almost month to month across 1931 — “wasted on children,” “a shame to waste it on children,” “too bad it is wasted on children” — before settling into the tight, proverb-like “youth is wasted on the young.” That drift is itself the tell: a genuine authored quotation tends to have one stable sentence, while a folk saying gets polished by every hand it passes through.

The sentiment does echo something Shaw actually wrote in Maxims for Revolutionists — “Youth, which is forgiven everything, forgives itself nothing; age, which forgives itself everything, is forgiven nothing” — which may be part of why his name stuck. But that is a resemblance, not the source.
context.pull: A stable sentence usually has an author; a saying that reshapes itself every few months usually has a newspaper.
